segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Well, I didn't have the modern conveyances that they have nowadays. They had the...just...worked out of character. I never knew anything to do with it. I didn't have the modern conveyances that they have nowadays.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I was thinking about how they cook. Do they all have wood stoves?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh yeah. Some of them had nothing with these wood stoves. They had four legs on each other and they set them high from the floor. And they had four legs on each other and they set them high from the floor. I didn't know that it burned cold and they didn't have any much blood on their heads. Those were shipped in. My mother always used that. Or she used wood. That's about all I know of. But anyway, the other chicks like her. The building of their building.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did she have the fire going all day?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Well, whenever she cooked. Something like baking bread. Oh, I think you know, the women nowadays, they didn't know how to bake a baker's bread. They didn't know what it was. Only once in a while, always. Oh, Dad's taking us to a restaurant, but we didn't have no restaurant them days. Only hotels, if you stayed in the hotel, you'd eat in the hotel dining room, but that's all. And taking us to a dining room or hotel, why, a hotel dining room, that was a treat.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would that be in the hotel in town?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Yes.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was that a very nice place to eat?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh, yes. Small little hotel. They had small hotels and then nice big places, of course. And then they had tablecloths. They didn't know what eating on the plain board table like it is now.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you get to go out to eat very much in those days?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Not very often. My mother, she did all the cooking and everything like that. We did the outside, milking cows and feeding calves and things like that. Herding hogs and I don't know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: That was all women's work?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Well, yeah, the women, they didn't think that was anything. No. You can't do that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Today you think of that as men's, just the work that men would do. You would think of women doing that kind of work, would you?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Well, I don't know. We didn't think much about it. I was about two years old, I remember all that. Out near the shed and she's out taking care of the cows, helping take care of the cows. I got near a calf and he knocked me down and I started crying and the cows started devolving. Because of the car commotion. I wasn't afraid of anything.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You weren't when you were growing up?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: I wasn't afraid of animals. Never.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When you were a kid then, did you spend, as a child, did you spend a lot of time with the livestock, the animals?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh, yes… no, we didn't think of anything.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was your mother concerned about you growing up to be a little lady?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh, yes. We could be a lady and be our own animals, too. She was frail, little one herself.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did that mean that the work that she had to do was hard on her because she was small?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh, we kept small, little one, you know, and she worked like everything… when she was a child at home, she had three brothers and one adopted brother and then… they took care of all the stuff on the outside. But when she married, then she had to learn how to feed calves and things like that, you know. We had a lot of work for her. Then we were kids, we learned how. My sister got on the outside of the fence, you know, and we helped the cow through the fence. And the cows, the calves were easy to rake into milk because we had to feed them in the calves, you know. They were tame and everything, so we learned how to learn how to milk them because they were tame. And then from then on, while they grew up, we broke them into milking. And then later on, why? Dad, he didn't buy them the cows anymore. He let us girls milk them. Mother had a square place in the cellar, she had a milk cellar with all the milk, so she kept a little milk in there. And a bill of rock and a mortar and all. And she kept all the milk pans in there and she just gave them all that cream all for the air. And they could make the butter and salad and take the milk to the hogs and skim milk. We stayed home all the time, we didn't know any different.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When you say you stayed home all the time, you mean that you didn't go around visiting other places and that kind of thing?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: No, we enjoyed ourselves at home, we didn't know the difference. Kids didn't know, kids didn't know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, did you, then, did you have much chance to play with other kids outside the family?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh yes, they'd come visit us, you know, neighbors and kids that way. It wasn't very many, very, very many days anyway.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you, when you were growing up, did you have a lot of different kinds of clothes or just a few pairs, a few outfits?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh, we didn't have many clothes, no. Mother bought the material and she'd make our clothes. Oh, you go to town, us kids are going in on the snow, how'd our mother go in? She'd buy the material and she'd take it home and make clothes for us girls.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were you, I was thinking about the kind of clothes that you wore, were they real long dresses and that kind of thing?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh yes, we went according to styles, you know, them days, you know, the work was just very long, wasn't dressed in all the wool and needs and we didn't know what coveralls were, you know. Wasn't really like to wear coveralls, I don't know, dresses.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you have dresses that you wore only for work?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: We had dresses for work and then we'd go to church so they wore some of their dress. We made a nice material and she sewed off on my eyes.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You know, I've heard it said that most women had one good black dress, is that true, will you remember it?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh, sometimes they had a black dress and mother, she never liked black, she never wore navy blue, serge. She was always so nice and so nice for us girls. She went to a program, her mother's average is quite young, she was a program school children, so all the dress patterns cut back chart. Not very gay people, we had to come home, it's not healthy, it's just like all of the art.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were you expected, Mrs. Jones, to do much work around the house or were you figured, were the girls...

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh, we used to play an awful lot and us children used to play an awful lot and we would help around the house and do things like that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What kind of things would you play when you were playing?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: We'd play house. Then we'd play with our horses and all, I don't know. And we didn't have the things to play with, toys and things, we didn't know what toys were, we just had a few things and we were satisfied with them. And we'd make mud pies and things like that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did kids fight with each other the way they do nowadays?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: No, they used to spank in school and we didn't know what fighting was, I guess.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you think you went to school when you went there?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh yes, I never got to start school until I was about nine years old. And then when I started eating, it was kind of hard for me, but I mean, I had a hard life, I liked it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Wait a minute, why was this, why did you wait until nine to start?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh, Dad was careless. We moved to town in Maryland from there to school then.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was there a school near you in the country where you went?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Yes, it was a parochial school and it was a public school.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What, in Genesee?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you go to parochial school?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Yes, part time… most of the time girls came from the water, but I don't think they came from the ocean, so I'll show you.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, I'm still wondering how it was that you didn't go out in the country, wasn't there a school nearby there?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: No, it was too far from each side, you see, the school, after Harley done away with them, no. They, we had to walk through school, you know, and then they got rid of the country schools and they just had the country schools and districts. And then the public school in Genesee.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, how far away were you in the country from the school?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Two and three quarter miles. And we'd have to walk there in the morning and we'd walk there in the evening. We'd be a little tired too.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So you didn't even go, you didn't go until you were nine.

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: No.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about your sisters?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: They were younger than I was. I don't know much about how far they were in school or anything. Children those days didn't go to school until late, until early.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, at nine, did you have to start in first grade?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh yes, but they had different methods, seven days at grade school and then they had the grade school and we had this, we started in little ABC books and then worked ourselves up.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, does that mean that you caught up before very long?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Is it bothering you to talk to your kids?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Well, I was in the country and of course when we were there Hawaii, we went to school and just continued just the same as now. And we got through and now we're not to work.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How old were you when you started to go out to work?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh, I don't remember.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you mean after school, in the afternoons or after you finished going to school, when you stopped going?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Well, I was, I don't remember.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: But you worked out?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What kind of work was that that you'd be doing for other people?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Well, I cooked ... cakes and waffles and then I worked at a table and I worked out twelve years before I was married.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I'm curious about the kind of work that you would do working out. Would you keep house for people?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh no.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: No?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: No, I never did any scrubbing or cleaning. I did restaurant work mostly, counter work. Like cooking hotcakes and waffles and answering the telephone, playing cashier.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: In Spokane this was?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did you think of that work?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh, I liked just clean work. I didn't have to put my hands on no dirty work or anything. Dishes and food and that's what it was all. Meet the public and answer the telephone, pay bills and do things like that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did you think of living in Spokane?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh, I liked it. It was alright.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How'd you happen to meet him?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh, he came in while I worked. I'm sorry to ...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Had he come from down here? Oh really? The wind is blowing.

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Yeah. He died just last week.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you go together for very long before you came?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Yeah, two or three years. Not that long I guess. Must have been about that long. Two or three years anyhow.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How did you happen to move back down to Genesee?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh, my daddy gave the proposition so I took it up and we stayed there, ready to craft. I raised lots of poultry and things like that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When you say proposition, what do you mean? He offered you to work on some of his land or what?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh, there's lots of buildings and things there. But he raised the crops and I raised the poultry and calves and milk cows and I made butter and solvents. It was a whole hard work.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You said your grandfather picked out your father for your mother. He picked him out for her. Is that the...

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Well, that's what they used to do in the early days. Mother was just a child and she was sixteen in October and they married in July. She was just a little frail girl.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did that mean that she didn't have any say so? He just told, said you're going to marry this fellow?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Oh, then they... Big enough at six or seven to milk cows. Well, the general knew that we didn't have a boy's job. Dad always handed back to her three times to finish milking. We had to go back and put a milking on. So, but we made it. I wish she had kept track of what she made, but she didn't.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Kept track of what she made? What do you mean?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Well, what she made out of butter and all. How much butter she sold and things like that. She never bought it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you say she made a lot?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Yeah, she paid the grocery bill.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: She paid the grocery bill?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Most of the time. Butter and eggs, she's a good butter maker. She had all her good luck making butter. She just seemed to come and match it for her. Well, she was Danish in the day. People were going to make butter, you know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Danish?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Born in Denmark. Or not born in Denmark, but she grew up. Her parents were born in Denmark and then she had... Had it covered on paper and she was born in the shoes and raised in this country. She's my girl with two brothers. And her mother died. Then he... Then him and the boys continued to the ranch and he took her when she was 11 years old to the pro -kill school at this ranch. And there she was five years and then she came out. And she was just past 16 when she got married. My grandfather thought that I was afraid of getting married. She was afraid of a little woman. I cooked off cake. She'd take some waffles. Three years before I was married.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Three years? In Spokane?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Yeah… in a place up there called Saddle Rock. And we had a big business up there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Saddle Rock?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: It was the name of the restaurant.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you know the people that ran it up there before you went? How'd you meet them?

segments.speaker: Agnes Healy Jones
segments.words: Well, I went up there to work and I asked them for work and they gave me work and they asked myself up. I got along fine. I married my husband and I moved down to my ranch and I raised poultry and stuff like that.
